problems.title: Mechanics – Problem I: Jumping particle
problems.statement:
A particle moves along the positive axis $Ox$ (one-dimensional situation) under a force that’s projection on $Ox$ is $F_x = F_0$ as represented in the figure below (as function of $x$ ). At the origin of $Ox$ axis is placed a perfectly reflecting wall.

A friction force of constant modulus $F_f = 1{,}00\ \mathrm{N}$ acts anywhere the particle is situated.

The particle starts from the point $x = x_0 = 1{,}00\ \mathrm{m}$ having the kinetic energy $E_c = 10{,}0\ \mathrm{J}$ .

figures.alt: Graph of the force F versus x: a hatched vertical wall at the origin 0, the x axis pointing right with the point x0 = 1,00 m marked on it, and a horizontal line at F0 = -10,0 N below the axis, continuing as a dashed line to the right.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find the length of the path of the particle before it comes to a final stop

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Sketch the potential energy $U(x)$ of the particle in the force field $F_x$ .

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Draw qualitatively the dependence of the particle speed as function of his coordinate $x$ .

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
It is possible to make a model of the situation in the problem, considering the $Ox$ axis vertically oriented having the wall in its’ lower part. The conservative force $F_x$ could be the weight of the particle. One may present the motion of the particle as the vertical motion of a small elastic ball elastically colliding with the ground and moving with constant friction through the medium. The friction force is smaller than the weight.

The potential energy of the particle can be represented in analogy to the gravitational potential energy of the ball, $mgh$, considering $mg=|F_x|$; $h=x$. As is very well known, in the field of a conservative force, the variation of the potential energy depends only on the initial and final positions of the particle, being independent of the path between those positions.

For the situation in the problem, when the particle moves towards the wall, the force acting on it is directed towards the wall and has the modulus

$$F_\leftarrow=|F_x|-F_f\tag{1.1}$$

$$F_\leftarrow=9\,\mathrm N.\tag{1.2}$$

As a consequence, the motion of the particle towards the wall is a motion with a constant acceleration having the modulus

$$a_\leftarrow=\frac{F_\leftarrow}m=\frac{|F_x|-F_f}m.\tag{1.3}$$

During the motion, the speed of the particle increases.

Hitting the wall, the particle starts moving in opposite direction with a speed equal in modulus with the one it had before the collision.

When the particle moves away from the wall, in the positive direction of the $Ox$ axis, the acting force is again directed towards to the wall and has the magnitude

$$F_\rightarrow=|F_x|+F_f\tag{1.4}$$

$$F_\rightarrow=11\,\mathrm N.\tag{1.5}$$

Correspondingly, the motion of the particle from the wall is slowed down and the magnitude of the acceleration is

$$a_\rightarrow=\frac{F_\rightarrow}m=\frac{|F_x|+F_f}m.\tag{1.6}$$

During this motion, the speed of the particle diminishes to zero.

Because during the motion a force acts on the particle, the body cannot have an equilibrium position in any point on axis – the origin making an exception as the potential energy vanishes there. The particle can definitively stop only in this point.

The work of a conservative force from the point having the coordinate $x_0=0$ to the point $x$, $L_{0\to x}$ is correlated with the variation of the potential energy of the particle $U(x)-U(0)$ as follows

$$\begin{aligned}U(x)-U(0)&=-L_{0\to x},\\U(x)-U(0)&=-\int_0^xF_x\,dx=\int_0^x|F_x|\,dx=|F_x|x.\end{aligned}\tag{1.7}$$

Admitting that the potential energy of the particle vanishes for $x=0$, the initial potential energy of the particle $U(x_0)$ in the field of conservative force

$$F_x(x)=F_0\tag{1.8}$$

can be written

$$U(x_0)=|F_0|x_0.\tag{1.9}$$

The initial kinetic energy $E(x_0)$ of the particle is – as given

$$E(x_0)=E_c\tag{1.10}$$

and, consequently the total energy of the particle $W(x_0)$ is

$$W(x_0)=U(x_0)+E_c.\tag{1.11}$$

The draw up of the particle occurs when the total energy of the particle is entirely exhausted by the work of the friction force. The distance covered by the particle before it stops, $D$, obeys

$$\begin{aligned}W(x_0)&=DF_f,\\U(x_0)+E_c&=DF_f,\\|F_x|x_0+E_c&=DF_f,\end{aligned}\tag{1.12}$$

so that,

$$D=\frac{|F_x|x_0+E_c}{F_f}\tag{1.13}$$

and

$$D=20\,\mathrm m.\tag{1.14}$$

The relations (1.13) and (1.14) represent the answer to the question I.a.

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
The relation (1.7) written as

$$U(x)=|F_x|x\tag{1.15}$$

gives the linear dependence of the potential energy to the position.

If the motion occurs without friction, the particle can reach a point $A$ situated at the distance $\delta$ apart from the origin in which the kinetic energy vanishes. In the point $A$ the energy of the particles is entirely potential.

The energy conservation law for the starting point and point $A$ gives

$$E_c+|F_x|x_0=|F_x|\delta,\qquad\delta=x_0+\frac{E_c}{|F_x|}.\tag{1.16}$$

The numerical value of the position of point $A$, furthest away from the origin, is $\delta=2\,\mathrm m$ if the motion occurs without friction.

The representation of the dependence of the potential energy on the position in the domain $(0,\delta)$ is represented in the figure 1.2.

![](p1-sol-fig1)

During the real motion of the particle (with friction) the extreme positions reached by the particle are smaller than $\delta$ (because of the leak of energy due to friction).

The graph in the figure 1.2 is the answer to the question I.b.

sections.title: c. Case 1
sections.statement:
During the motion of the particle its energy decrease because of the dissipation work of the friction force. The speed of the particle has a local maximum near the wall. Denoting $v_k$ the speed of the particle just before its’ $k$th collision with the wall and $v_{k+1}$ the speed just before its’ next collision, $v_k>v_{k+1}$.

Among two successive collisions, the particle reaches its’ $x_k$ positions in which its’ speed vanishes and the energy of the particle is purely potential. These positions are closer and closer to the wall because a part of the energy of the particle is dissipated through friction.

$$x_{k+1}<x_k.\tag{1.17}$$

When the particle moves towards the wall, both its’ speed and its’ kinetic energy increases. The potential energy of the particle decreases. During the motion – independent of its’ direction- energy is dissipated through the friction force.

The potential energy of the particle, $U(x)$, the kinetic energy $E(x)$ and the total energy of the particle during this part of the motion $W(x)$ obey the relation

$$W(x_0)-W(x)=F_f(x_0-x),\tag{1.18}$$

the position $x$ lying in the domain

$$x\in(0,x_0)\tag{1.19}$$

covered from $x_0$ towards origin. The relation (1.18) can be written as

$$[E_c+|F_x|x_0]-\left[\frac{mv^2}2+|F_x|x\right]=F_f(x_0-x),\tag{1.20}$$

so that

$$\begin{aligned}v^2&=\frac2m[E_c+|F_x|x_0-|F_x|x-F_f(x_0-x)],\\v^2&=\frac2m[E_c+x_0(|F_x|-F_f)-x(|F_x|-F_f)]\end{aligned}\tag{1.21}$$

and by consequence

$$v=-\sqrt{\frac2m[E_c+x_0(|F_x|-F_f)-x(|F_x|-F_f)]}.\tag{1.22}$$

The minus sign in front of the magnitude of the speed indicates that the motion of the particle occurs into the negative direction of the coordinate axis.

Using the problem data

$$v^2=\frac2m(19-9x),\qquad v=-\sqrt{\frac2m(19-9x)}.\tag{1.23}$$

The speed of the particle at the first collision with the wall $v_{1\leftarrow}$ can be written as

$$v_{1\leftarrow}=-\sqrt{\frac2m[E_c+x_0(|F_x|-F_f)]}\tag{1.24}$$

and has the value

$$v_{1\leftarrow}=-\sqrt{\frac2m19}.\tag{1.25}$$

The total energy near the wall, purely kinetic $E_{1\leftarrow}$, has the expression

$$E_{1\leftarrow}=E_c+x_0(|F_x|-F_f).\tag{1.26}$$

The numerical value of this energy is

$$E_{1\leftarrow}=19\,\mathrm J.\tag{1.27}$$

The graph in the figure (1.3) gives the dependence on position of the square of the speed for the first part of the particle’s motion.

![](p1-sol-fig2)

![](p1-sol-fig3)

The graph in the figure (1.4) presents the speed’s dependence on the position in this first part of the particle’s motion (towards the wall).

After the collision with the wall, the speed of the particle, $v_{1\rightarrow}$, has the same magnitude as the speed just before the collision but it is directed in the opposite way. In the graphical representation of the speed as a function of position, the collision with the wall is represented as a jump of the speed from a point lying on negative side of the speed axis to a point lying on positive side of the speed axis. The absolute value of the speed just before and immediately after the collision is the same as represented in the figure 1.5.

$$v_{1\rightarrow}=\sqrt{\frac2m[E_c+x_0(|F_x|-F_f)]}.\tag{1.28}$$

After the first collision, the motion of the particle is slowed down with a constant deceleration $a_\rightarrow$ and an initial speed $v_{1\rightarrow}$. This motion continues to the position $x_1$ where the speed vanishes. From Galileo law it can be inferred that

$$\begin{aligned}0&=v_{1\rightarrow}^2-2a_\rightarrow x_1,\\x_1&=\frac{v_{1\rightarrow}^2}{2a_\rightarrow}=\frac{\frac2m[E_c+x_0(|F_x|-F_f)]}{2\frac{|F_x|+F_f}m}=\frac{E_c+x_0(|F_x|-F_f)}{|F_x|+F_f}.\end{aligned}\tag{1.29}$$

The numerical value of the position $x_1$ is

$$x_1=\frac{19}{11}\,\mathrm m.\tag{1.30}$$

For the positions

$$x\in(0,x_1)\tag{1.31}$$

covered from the origin towards $x_1$ the total energy $W(x)$ has the expression

$$W(x)=\frac{mv^2}2+|F_x|x.\tag{1.32}$$

From the wall, the energy of the particle diminishes because of the friction – that is

$$\begin{aligned}E_{1\leftarrow}-W(x)&=F_fx,\\E_c+x_0(|F_x|-F_f)-\frac{mv^2}2-|F_x|x&=F_fx.\end{aligned}\tag{1.33}$$

The square of the magnitude of the speed is

$$\begin{aligned}v^2&=\frac2m[E_c+x_0(|F_x|-F_f)-(|F_x|+F_f)x],\\v^2&=\frac2m(|F_x|+F_f)(x_1-x)\end{aligned}\tag{1.34}$$

and the speed is

$$v=\sqrt{\frac2m[E_c+x_0(|F_x|-F_f)-(|F_x|+F_f)x]}.\tag{1.35}$$

Using the furnished data results

$$v^2=\frac2m[19-11x]\tag{1.36}$$

and respectively

$$v=\sqrt{\frac2m[19-11x]}.\tag{1.37}$$

For the positions lying in the domain $x\in(0,x_1)$ - (which correspond to a second part of the motion of particle) the figure 1.5 gives the dependence of the speed on the position.

![](p1-sol-fig4)

As can be observed in the figure, after reaching the furthest away position, $x_1$, the particle moves towards the origin, without an initial speed, in an accelerated motion having an acceleration with the magnitude of $a_\leftarrow=(|F_x|-F_f)/m$. After the collision with the wall, the particle has a velocity equal in magnitude but opposite in direction with the one it had just before the collision.

When the particle reaches a point in the domain $(0,x_1)$ moving from $x_1$ towards the origin its’ total energy $W(x)$ has the expression (1.32).

Starting from $x_1$, because of the dissipation determined by the friction force, the energy changes to the value corresponding to the position with coordinate $x$.

$$|F_x|x_1-W(x)=F_f(x_1-x),\qquad |F_x|x_1-\frac{mv^2}2-|F_x|x=F_f(x_1-x).\tag{1.38}$$

The square of the speed has the expression

$$\begin{aligned}v^2&=\frac2m[(|F_x|-F_f)(x_1-x)],\\v^2&=\frac2m\left[\frac{E_c+x_0(|F_x|-F_f)}{|F_x|+F_f}-x\right](|F_x|-F_f)\end{aligned}\tag{1.39}$$

and the speed is

$$v=\sqrt{\frac2m\left[\frac{E_c+x_0(|F_x|-F_f)}{|F_x|+F_f}-x\right](|F_x|-F_f)}.\tag{1.40}$$

Using the given data, for a position in the domain $(0,x_1)$

$$v^2=\frac2m\left[\frac{19}{11}-x\right]9\tag{1.41}$$

respectively

$$v=-\sqrt{\frac2m\left[\frac{19}{11}-x\right]9}.\tag{1.42}$$

The speed of the particle when it reaches for the second time the wall has - using (1.39) - the expression

$$v_{2\leftarrow}=-\sqrt{\frac2m\left\{\frac{E_c+x_0(|F_x|-F_f)}{|F_x|+F_f}(|F_x|-F_f)\right\}}.\tag{1.43}$$

The resulting numerical value is

$$v_{2\leftarrow}=-\sqrt{\frac2m\frac{171}{11}}.\tag{1.44}$$

Concluding, after the first collision and first recoil, the particle moves away from the wall, reaches again a position where the speed vanishes and then comes back to the wall. The speed of the particle hitting again the wall is smaller than before – as in the figure 1.5.

As it was denoted before $v_k$ is the speed of the particle just before its’ $k$th run and $x_k$ is the coordinate of the furthest away point reached during the $k$th run. The energy of the particle starting from the wall is

$$E_k=\frac{v_k^2m}2=W_k(0).\tag{1.45}$$

In the point $x_k$, the furthest away from the origin after $k$th collision, the energy verifies the relation

$$U_k=x_k|F_x|=W_k(x_k).\tag{1.46}$$

The variation of the energy between starting point and point $x_k$ is

$$\frac{v_k^2m}2-x_k|F_x|=F_fx_k,\tag{1.47}$$

so that

$$x_k=\frac{v_k^2m}{2(|F_x|+F_f)}.\tag{1.48}$$

After the particle reaches point $x_k$ the direction of the speed changes and, when the particle reaches again the wall

$$\frac{v_{k+1}^2m}2=E_{k+1}=W_{k+1}(0).\tag{1.49}$$

The energy conservation law for the $x_k$ point and the state when the particle reaches again the wall gives

$$x_k|F_x|-\frac{v_{k+1}^2m}2=F_fx_k,\tag{1.50}$$

so that

$$v_{k+1}^2=\frac2mx_k(|F_x|-F_f).\tag{1.51}$$

Considering (1.48), the relation (1.51) becomes

$$v_{k+1}^2=v_k^2\frac{|F_x|-F}{|F_x|+F}.\tag{1.52}$$

Between two consequent collisions the speed diminishes in a geometrical progression having the ratio $q$. This ratio has the expression

$$q=\sqrt{\frac{|F_x|-F}{|F_x|+F}}\tag{1.53}$$

and the value

$$q=\sqrt{\frac9{11}}.\tag{1.54}$$

For the $k+1$ collision the relation (1.48) becomes

$$x_{k+1}=\frac{v_{k+1}^2m}{2(|F_x|+F_f)}.\tag{1.55}$$

Taking into account (1.52), the ratio of the successive extreme positions can be written as

$$\frac{x_{k+1}}{x_k}=\frac{|F_x|-F_f}{|F_x|+F_f}=q^2,\qquad x_{k+1}=q^2x_k.\tag{1.56}$$

From the $k$ run towards origin, (analogous to (1.39)), the dependence of the square of the speed on position can be written as $v_{(k,\leftarrow)}^2$

$$v_{(k,\leftarrow)}^2=\frac2m[(|F_x|-F_f)(x_k-x)],\qquad v_{(k,\leftarrow)}^2=\frac2m[(|F_x|-F_f)(x_1q^{2k}-x)]\tag{1.57}$$

or, using the data

$$v_{(k,\leftarrow)}^2=\frac2m\left[9\left(\frac{19}{11}\left(\frac9{11}\right)^k-x\right)\right].\tag{1.58}$$

For the $k$th run from the origin (analogous with (1.34)), the dependence on the position of the square of the magnitude of the speed $v_{(k,\rightarrow)}^2$ can be written as

$$v_{(k,\rightarrow)}^2=\frac2m[(|F_x|+F_f)(x_k-x)],\qquad v_{(k,\rightarrow)}^2=\frac2m[(|F_x|+F_f)(x_1q^{2k}-x)].\tag{1.59}$$

Using given data

$$v_{(k,\rightarrow)}^2=\frac2m\left[11\left(\frac{19}{11}\left(\frac9{11}\right)^k-x\right)\right].\tag{1.60}$$

The evolution of the square of the speed as function of position is represented in the figure 1.6.

![](p1-sol-fig5)

And the evolution of the speed as function of position is represented in the figure 1.7.

![](p1-sol-fig6)

The sum of the progression given in (1.56) gives half of the distance covered by the particle after the first collision.

$$\sum_{k=1}^\infty x_k=x_1\frac1{1-q^2}.\tag{1.61}$$

Considering (1.53) and (1.29)

$$\sum_{k=1}^\infty x_k=\frac{E_c+x_0(|F_x|-F_f)}{2F_f}.\tag{1.62}$$

Numerically,

$$\sum_{k=1}^\infty x_k=\frac{19}2\,\mathrm m.\tag{1.63}$$

The total covered distance is

$$D=2\sum_{k=1}^\infty x_k+x_0,\qquad D=20\,\mathrm m,\tag{1.64}$$

which is the same with (1.14).

sections.title: c. Case 2
sections.statement:
If the particle starts from the $x_0$ position moving in the positive direction of the coordinate axis $Ox$ its’ speed diminishes and its’ kinetic energy also diminishes while its’ potential energy increases to a maximum in the $x_1'$ position where the speed vanishes. During this motion the energy is dissipated due to the friction.

The total energy $W(x)$, for the positions $x$ between $x_0$ and $x_1'$ verify the relation

$$W(x_0)-W(x)=F_f(x-x_0),\tag{1.65}$$

the position $x$ lying in the domain

$$x\in(x_0,x_1')\tag{1.66}$$

when the particle moves from $x_0$ in the positive direction of the axis. The relation (1.65) becomes

$$[E_c+|F_x|x_0]-\left[\frac{mv^2}2+|F_x|x\right]=F_f(x-x_0),\tag{1.67}$$

so that

$$\begin{aligned}v^2&=\frac2m[E_c+|F_x|x_0-|F_x|x-F_f(x-x_0)],\\v^2&=\frac2m[E_c+x_0(|F_x|+F_f)-x(|F_x|+F_f)]\end{aligned}\tag{1.68}$$

and

$$v=\sqrt{\frac2m[E_c+x_0(|F_x|+F_f)-x(|F_x|+F_f)]}.\tag{1.69}$$

Using provided data

$$v^2=\frac2m(21-11x),\qquad v=\sqrt{\frac2m(21-11x)}.\tag{1.70}$$

![](p1-sol-fig7)

![](p1-sol-fig8)

The graph in the figure (1.8) presents the dependence of the square speed on the position for the motion in the domain $x\in(x_0,x_1')$. The particle moves in the positive direction of the coordinate axis $Ox$.

This motion occurs until the position $x_1'$ - when the speed vanishes - is reached. From the relation (1.68), in which we take the modulus of the speed zero, results

$$x_1'=x_0+\frac{E_c}{|F_x|+F_f}.\tag{1.71}$$

The numerical value for $x_1'$ is

$$x_1'=\frac{21}{11}\,\mathrm m.\tag{1.72}$$

After furthest away position $x_1'$ is reached, the particle moves again towards the origin, without initial speed, in a speeded up motion having an acceleration of magnitude $a_\leftarrow=(|F_x|-F_f)/m$. After the collision with the wall, the particle has a velocity $v_{1\rightarrow}'$ equal in magnitude but opposite direction with the one it had before the collision $v_{1\leftarrow}'$.

When the particle is at a point lying in the domain $(0,x_1')$ running from $x_1'$ to the origin, its’ total energy $W(x)$ has the expression

$$W(x)=\frac{mv^2}2+|F_x|x.\tag{1.73}$$

Because of friction, the value of the energy decreases from the one it had at $x_1'$ to the corresponding to the $x$ position

$$|F_x|x_1'-W(x)=F_f(x_1'-x),\qquad |F_x|x_1'-\frac{mv^2}2-|F_x|x=F_f(x_1'-x).\tag{1.74}$$

The square of the speed has the expression

$$v^2=\frac2m[(|F_x|-F_f)(x_1'-x)]\tag{1.75}$$

and the speed is

$$v=-\sqrt{\frac2m[(|F_x|-F_f)(x_1'-x)]}.\tag{1.76}$$

For the given data, in the domain, $(0,x_1')$

$$v^2=\frac2m\left[\frac{21}{11}-x\right]9\tag{1.77}$$

respectively

$$v=-\sqrt{\frac2m\left[\frac{21}{11}-x\right]9}.\tag{1.78}$$

The speed of the particle hitting a second time the wall is – according to (1.78)-

$$v_{1\leftarrow}'=-\sqrt{\frac2m[(|F_x|-F_f)x_1']}\tag{1.79}$$

and has the value

$$v_{1\leftarrow}'=-\sqrt{\frac2m\frac{189}{11}}.\tag{1.80}$$

Concluding, after the first collision and first recoil, the particle moves away from the wall, reaches again a position where the speed vanishes and then comes back to the wall. The speed of the particle hitting again the wall is smaller than before – as in the figure 1.11.

Denoting $v_k'$ the speed at the beginning of the $k$th run and $x_k'$ the coordinate of the furthest away point during the $k$th run, the energy of the particle leaving the wall is

$$E_k'=\frac{v_k'^2m}2=W_k'(0).\tag{1.81}$$

In the position $x_k'$ after the $k$ departure from the wall, the energy is

$$U_k'=x_k'|F_x|=W_k'(x_k').\tag{1.82}$$

The variation of the total energy has the expression

$$\frac{v_k'^2m}2-x_k'|F_x|=F_fx_k',\tag{1.83}$$

so that

$$x_k'=\frac{v_k'^2m}{2(|F_x|+F_f)}.\tag{1.84}$$

After the particle reaches the position $x_k'$ the direction of the speed changes and, when the particle hits the wall,

$$\frac{v_{k+1}'^2m}2=E_{k+1}'=W_{k+1}'(0).\tag{1.85}$$

The energy conservation law for the $x_k'$ position and the point in which the particle hits the wall gives

$$x_k'|F_x|-\frac{v_{k+1}'^2m}2=F_fx_k',\tag{1.86}$$

so that

$$v_{k+1}'^2=\frac2mx_k'(|F_x|-F_f).\tag{1.87}$$

Considering (1.84), the relation (1.87) becomes

$$v_{k+1}'^2=v_k'^2\frac{|F_x|-F}{|F_x|+F}.\tag{1.88}$$

Between two successive collisions the speed diminishes in a geometrical progression with the ratio $q$

$$q=\sqrt{\frac{|F_x|-F}{|F_x|+F}}.\tag{1.89}$$

Using the data provided

$$q=\sqrt{\frac9{11}}.\tag{1.90}$$

From $(k+1)$th, collision the relation (1.84) is written as

$$x_{k+1}'=\frac{v_{k+1}'^2m}{2(|F_x|+F_f)}.\tag{1.91}$$

Considering (1.84) and (1.91), the ratio of the extreme positions in two successive runs is

$$\frac{x_{k+1}'}{x_k'}=\frac{|F_x|-F_f}{|F_x|+F_f}=q^2,\qquad x_{k+1}'=q^2x_k'.\tag{1.92}$$

For the $k$th run towards the origin, analogous to (1.57), one may write the dependence of the square speed $v_{(k,\leftarrow)}'^2$ as function of the position as

$$v_{(k,\leftarrow)}'^2=\frac2m[(|F_x|-F_f)(x_k'-x)],\qquad v_{(k,\leftarrow)}'^2=\frac2m[(|F_x|-F_f)(x_1'q^{2k}-x)].\tag{1.93}$$

Or, using the data

$$v_{(k,\leftarrow)}'^2=\frac2m\left[9\left(\frac{21}{11}\left(\frac9{11}\right)^k-x\right)\right].\tag{1.94}$$

From the $k$th run from the origin, analogous to (1.59), the dependence on the position of the square speed $v_{(k,\rightarrow)}^2$ can be written as

$$v_{(k,\rightarrow)}'^2=\frac2m[(|F_x|+F_f)(x_k'-x)],\qquad v_{(k,\rightarrow)}'^2=\frac2m[(|F_x|+F_f)(x_1'q^{2k}-x)].\tag{1.95}$$

Using given data

$$v_{(k,\rightarrow)}'^2=\frac2m\left[11\left(\frac{21}{11}\left(\frac9{11}\right)^k-x\right)\right].\tag{1.96}$$

The evolution of the square of the speed as function on position is presented in the figure 1.10.

![](p1-sol-fig9)

And the evolution of the speed as function of the position is presented in the figure 1.11.

![](p1-sol-fig10)

The sum of the geometrical progression (1.92) gives (after the doubling and then subtracting of the $x_0$) the total distance covered by the particle.

$$\sum_{k=1}^\infty x_k'=x_1'\frac1{1-q^2}.\tag{1.97}$$

Considering (1.97), (1.71) and (1.72) it results

$$\sum_{k=1}^\infty x_k'=\frac{21}2\,\mathrm m.\tag{1.98}$$

The total distance covered by the particle is

$$D=2\sum_{k=1}^\infty x_k'-x_0,\qquad D=20\,\mathrm m,\tag{1.99}$$

which allows us to find again the result (1.14).

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
As is very well known in the study of AC circuits using the formalism of complex numbers, a complex inductive reactance $\bar X_L=L\omega j$, $(j=\sqrt{-1})$ is attached to the inductance $L$ - part of a circuit supplied with an alternative current having the pulsation $\omega$. Similar, a complex capacitive reactance $\bar X_C=-j/(C\omega)$ is attached to the capacity $C$. A parallel circuit will be characterized by his complex admittance $\bar Y$. The admittance of the AC circuit represented in the figure is

$$\begin{aligned}\bar Y&=\frac1R+\frac1{L_1\omega j}+\frac1{L_2\omega j}-\frac{C_1\omega}j-\frac{C_2\omega}j\\&=\frac1R+j\left[(C_1+C_2)-\left(\frac1{L_1}+\frac1{L_2}\right)\right].\end{aligned}\tag{2.1}$$

The circuit behave as if has a parallel equivalent capacity $C$

$$C=C_1+C_2\tag{2.2}$$

and a parallel equivalent inductance $L$

$$\frac1L=\frac1{L_1}+\frac1{L_2},\qquad L=\frac{L_1L_2}{L_1+L_2},\tag{2.3}$$

The complex admittance of the circuit may be written as

$$\bar Y=\frac1R+j\left(C\omega-\frac1{L\omega}\right).\tag{2.4}$$

and the complex impedance of the circuit will be

$$\bar Z=\frac1{\bar Y}=\frac{\frac1R+j(\frac1{L\omega}-C\omega)}{\sqrt{(\frac1R)^2+(C\omega-\frac1{L\omega})^2}}.\tag{2.5}$$

The impedance $Z$ of the circuit, the inverse of the admittance of the circuit $Y$ is the modulus of the complex impedance $\bar Z$

$$Z=|\bar Z|=\frac1{\sqrt{(\frac1R)^2+(C\omega-\frac1{L\omega})^2}}=\frac1Y.\tag{2.6}$$

The constant current source supplying the circuit furnish a current having a momentary value $i(t)$

$$i=I\sqrt2\sin\omega t,\tag{2.7}$$

where $I$ is the effective intensity (constant), of the current and $\omega$ is the current pulsation (that can vary). The potential difference at the jacks of the circuit has the momentary value $u(t)$

$$u=U\sqrt2\sin(\omega t+\varphi).\tag{2.8}$$

where $U$ is the effective value of the tension and $\varphi$ is the phase difference between tension and current.

The effective values of the current and tension obey the relation

$$U=IZ.\tag{2.9}$$

The active power in the circuit is

$$P=\frac{U^2}R=\frac{Z^2I^2}R,\tag{2.10}$$

Because as in the enounce,

$$I=\text{constant},\qquad R=\text{constant}.\tag{2.11}$$

the maximal active power is realized for the maximum value of the impedance that is the minimal value of the admittance. The admittance

$$Y=\sqrt{\left(\frac1R\right)^2+\left(C\omega-\frac1{L\omega}\right)^2}.\tag{2.12}$$

has– as function of the pulsation $\omega$ - an „the smallest value”

$$Y_{\min}=\frac1R\tag{2.13}$$

for the pulsation

$$\omega_m=\frac1{\sqrt{LC}},\tag{2.14}$$

In this case

$$C\omega-\frac1{L\omega}=0.\tag{2.15}$$

So, the minimal active power in the circuit has the value

$$P_m=RI^2.\tag{2.16}$$

and occurs in the situation of alternative current furnished by the source at the frequency $f_m$

$$f_m=\frac{\omega_m}{2\pi}=\frac1{2\pi\sqrt{CL}}.\tag{2.17}$$

To ensure that the active power is half of the maximum power it is necessary that

$$P=\frac12P_m,\qquad\frac{Z^2I^2}R=\frac12RI^2,\qquad\frac2{R^2}=\frac1{Z^2}=Y^2.\tag{2.18}$$

That is

$$\frac2{R^2}=\frac1{R^2}+\left(C\omega-\frac1{L\omega}\right)^2,\qquad\pm\frac1R=C\omega-\frac1{L\omega}.\tag{2.19}$$

The pulsation of the current ensuring an active power at half of the maximum power must satisfy one of the equations

$$\omega^2\pm\frac\omega{RC}-\frac1{LC}=0.\tag{2.20}$$

The two second degree equation may furnish the four solutions

$$\omega=\pm\frac1{2RC}\pm\frac12\sqrt{\left(\frac1{RC}\right)^2+\frac4{LC}}.\tag{2.21}$$

Because the pulsation is every time positive, and because

$$\sqrt{\left(\frac1{RC}\right)^2+\frac4{LC}}>\frac1{RC},\tag{2.22}$$

the only two valid solutions are

$$\omega_\pm=\frac12\sqrt{\left(\frac1{RC}\right)^2+\frac4{LC}}\pm\frac1{2RC}.\tag{2.23}$$

It exist two frequencies $f_\pm=\omega_\pm/(2\pi)$ allowing to obtain in the circuit an active power representing half of the maximum power.

$$f_+=\frac1{2\pi}\left(\frac12\sqrt{\left(\frac1{RC}\right)^2+\frac4{LC}}+\frac1{2RC}\right),\qquad f_-=\frac1{2\pi}\left(\frac12\sqrt{\left(\frac1{RC}\right)^2+\frac4{LC}}-\frac1{2RC}\right).\tag{2.24}$$

The difference of these frequencies is

$$\Delta f=f_+-f_-=\frac1{2\pi RC}.\tag{2.25}$$

the bandwidth of the circuit – the frequency interval around the resonance frequency having at the ends a signal representing $1/\sqrt2$ from the resonance signal. At the ends of the bandwidth the active power reduces at the half of his value at the resonance. The asked ratio is

$$\frac{f_m}{\Delta f}=\frac{RC}{\sqrt{LC}}=R\sqrt{\frac CL}=R\sqrt{\frac{(C_1+C_2)(L_1+L_2)}{L_1L_2}}.\tag{2.26}$$

With $C=15\,\mathrm{nF}$, $L=\frac{20}3\,\mathrm{mH}$ and $\omega_m=10^5\,\mathrm{rad/s}$,

$$\frac{f_m}{\Delta f}=R\sqrt{\frac CL}=100\times10^3\sqrt{\frac{3\cdot15\times10^{-9}}{20\times10^{-3}}}=150.\tag{2.27}$$

The (2.26) relation is the answer at the question a.

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
The fact that immediately after the source is detached it is a current in the coils, allow as to admit that currents dependents on time will continue to flow through the coils.

![](p2-sol-fig1)

The capacitors will be charged with charges variable in time. The variation of the charges of the capacitors will results in currents flowing through the conductors linking the capacitors in the circuit. The momentary tension on the jacks of the coils and capacitors – identical for all elements in circuit – is also dependent on time. Let’s admit that the electrical potential of the points $C$ and $D$ is $u(t)$ and the potential of the points $A$ and $B$ is zero. If through the inductance $L_1$ passes the variable current having the momentary value $i_1(t)$, the relation between the current and potentials is

$$u-L_1\frac{di_1}{dt}=0,\tag{2.28}$$

The current passing through the second inductance $i_2(t)$ has the expression,

$$u-L_2\frac{di_2}{dt}=0.\tag{2.29}$$

If on the positive plate of the capacitor having the capacity $C_1$ is stocked the charge $q_1(t)$, then at the jacks of the capacitor the electrical tension is $u(t)$ and

$$q_1=C_1u,\tag{2.30}$$

Deriving this relation it results

$$\frac{dq_1}{dt}=C_1\frac{du}{dt},\tag{2.31}$$

But

$$\frac{dq_1}{dt}=-i_3,\tag{2.32}$$

because the electrical current appears because of the diminishing of the electrical charge on capacitor plate. Consequently

$$i_3=-C_1\frac{du}{dt}.\tag{2.33}$$

Analogous, for the other capacitor,

$$i_4=-C_4\frac{du}{dt}.\tag{2.34}$$

Considering all obtained results

$$\frac{di_1}{dt}=\frac u{L_1},\qquad\frac{di_2}{dt}=\frac u{L_2},\tag{2.35}$$

respectively

$$\frac{di_3}{dt}=-C_1\frac{d^2u}{dt^2},\qquad\frac{di_4}{dt}=C_2\frac{d^2u}{dt^2}.\tag{2.36}$$

Denoting $i_5(t)$ the momentary intensity of the current flowing from point $B$ to the point $A$, then the same momentary intensity has the current through the points $C$ and $D$. For the point $A$ the Kirchhoff rule of the currents gives

$$i_1+i_5=i_3,\tag{2.37}$$

For $B$ point the same rule produces

$$i_4+i_5=i_2.\tag{2.38}$$

Considering (2.37) and (2.38) results

$$i_1-i_3=i_4-i_2,\tag{2.39}$$

and deriving

$$\frac{di_1}{dt}-\frac{di_3}{dt}=\frac{di_4}{dt}-\frac{di_2}{dt}.\tag{2.40}$$

that is

$$-\frac u{L_1}-\frac u{L_2}=C_1\frac{d^2u}{dt^2}+C_2\frac{d^2u}{dt^2},\qquad-u\left(\frac1{L_1}+\frac1{L_2}\right)=\frac{d^2u}{dt^2}(C_1+C_2).\tag{2.41}$$

Using the symbols defined above

$$-\frac uL=C\frac{d^2u}{dt^2},\qquad\ddot u+\frac1{LC}u=0.\tag{2.42}$$

Because the tension obeys the relation above, it must have a harmonic dependence on time

$$u=A\sin(\omega t+\delta),\tag{2.43}$$

The pulsation of the tension is

$$\omega=\frac1{\sqrt{LC}}.\tag{2.44}$$

Taking into account the relations (2.43) and (2.36) it results that

$$i_3=-C_1\frac d{dt}(A\sin(\omega t+\delta))=-C_1A\omega\cos(\omega t+\delta),\qquad i_4=-C_2\frac d{dt}(A\sin(\omega t+\delta))=-C_2A\omega\cos(\omega t+\delta).\tag{2.45}$$

and

$$\frac{di_1}{dt}=\frac u{L_1}=\frac A{L_1}\sin(\omega t+\delta),\qquad\frac{di_2}{dt}=\frac u{L_2}=\frac A{L_2}\sin(\omega t+\delta).\tag{2.46}$$

It results that

$$i_1=\frac A{L_1\omega}\cos(\omega t+\delta)+M,\qquad i_2=\frac A{L_2\omega}\cos(\omega t+\delta)+N.\tag{2.47}$$

In the expression above, $A$, $M$, $N$ and $\delta$ are constants that must be determined using initially conditions. It is remarkable that the currents through capacitors are sinusoidal but the currents through the coils are the sum of sinusoidal and constant currents. In the first moment

$$u(0)=u_0=40\,\mathrm V,\qquad i_1(0)=i_{01}=0.1\,\mathrm A,\qquad i_2(0)=i_{02}=0.2\,\mathrm A.\tag{2.48}$$

Because the values of the inductances and capacities are

$$L_1=0.01\,\mathrm H,\quad L_2=0.02\,\mathrm H,\quad C_1=10\,\mathrm{nF},\quad C_2=5\,\mathrm{nF}.\tag{2.49}$$

the equivalent inductance and capacity is

$$\frac1L=\frac1{L_1}+\frac1{L_2},\qquad L=\frac{L_1L_2}{L_1+L_2}=\frac{2\times10^{-4}}{3\times10^{-2}}\,\mathrm H=\frac1{150}\,\mathrm H,\tag{2.50}$$

respectively

$$C=C_1+C_2=15\,\mathrm{nF}.\tag{2.51}$$

From (2.44) results

$$\omega=\frac1{\sqrt{\frac1{150}\cdot15\times10^{-9}}}=10^5\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}},\tag{2.52}$$

The value of the pulsation allows calculating the value of the requested frequency b. This frequency has the value $f$

$$f=\frac\omega{2\pi}=\frac{10^5}{2\pi}\,\mathrm{Hz}.\tag{2.53}$$

sections.title: c.
sections.statement:
If the momentary tension on circuit is like in (2.43), one may write

$$u(0)=A\sin\delta=u_0,\qquad\sin\delta=\frac{u_0}A.\tag{2.54}$$

From the currents (2.47) is possible to write

$$i_{01}=\frac A{L_1\omega}\cos\delta+M,\qquad i_{02}=\frac A{L_2\omega}\cos\delta+N.\tag{2.55}$$

On the other side is possible to express (2.39) as

$$\begin{aligned}i_1-i_3&=i_4-i_2,\\\frac A{L_1\omega}\cos(\omega t+\delta)+M+C_1A\omega\cos(\omega t+\delta)&=-C_2A\omega\cos(\omega t+\delta)-\frac A{L_2\omega}\cos(\omega t+\delta)-N.\end{aligned}\tag{2.56}$$

An identity as

$$A\cos\alpha+B\equiv C\cos\alpha+D\tag{2.57}$$

is valuable for any value of the argument $\alpha$ only if

$$A=C,\qquad B=D.\tag{2.58}$$

Considering (2.58), from (2.56) it results

$$M+N=0,\qquad A\omega(C_1+C_2)=-\frac A\omega\left(\frac1{L_1}+\frac1{L_2}\right).\tag{2.59}$$

For the last equation it results that the circuit oscillate with the pulsation in the relation (2.44). Adding relations (2.55) and considering (2.54) and (2.59) results that

$$\begin{aligned}i_{01}+i_{02}&=A\cos\delta\,\frac1\omega\left(\frac1{L_1}+\frac1{L_1}\right),\\A&=\frac{i_{01}+i_{02}}{\cos\delta\,\frac1\omega(\frac1{L_1}+\frac1{L_1})},\\\cos\delta&=\frac{i_{01}+i_{02}}{A\frac1\omega(\frac1{L_1}+\frac1{L_1})},\\\cos\delta&=\frac{(i_{01}+i_{02})L\omega}A.\end{aligned}\tag{2.60}$$

The numerical value of the amplitude of the electrical tension results by summing the last relations from (2.54) and (2.60)

$$\begin{aligned}\sin\delta&=\frac{u_0}A,\\\cos\delta&=\frac{(i_{01}+i_{02})L\omega}A,\\(\cos\delta)^2+(\sin\delta)^2&=1,\\\left(\frac{u_0}A\right)^2+\left(\frac{(i_{01}+i_{02})L\omega}A\right)^2&=1,\\A&=\sqrt{u_0^2+((i_{01}+i_{02})L\omega)^2}.\end{aligned}\tag{2.61}$$

The numerical value of the electrical tension on the jacks of the circuit is

$$A=\sqrt{40^2+(0.3\cdot\tfrac1{150}\cdot10^5)^2}=\sqrt{40^2+200^2}=40\sqrt{26}\,\mathrm V.\tag{2.62}$$

And consequently from (2.54) results

$$\sin\delta=\frac{u_0}A=\frac{40}{40\sqrt{26}}=\frac1{\sqrt{26}}\tag{2.63}$$

and

$$\cos\delta=\frac5{\sqrt{26}}.\tag{2.64}$$

Also

$$\operatorname{tg}\delta=\frac15,\qquad\delta=\operatorname{arctg}(1/5).\tag{2.65}$$

From (2.55)

$$M=i_{01}-\frac A{L_1\omega}\cos\delta,\qquad N=i_{02}-\frac A{L_2\omega}\cos\delta,\tag{2.66}$$

the corresponding numerical values are

$$\begin{aligned}M&=\left(0.1-\frac1{0.01\cdot10^5}\,40\sqrt{26}\,\frac5{\sqrt{26}}\right)\mathrm A=-0.1\,\mathrm A,\\N&=\left(0.2-\frac1{0.02\cdot10^5}\,40\sqrt{26}\,\frac5{\sqrt{26}}\right)\mathrm A=0.1\,\mathrm A.\end{aligned}\tag{2.67}$$

The relations (2.47) becomes

$$\begin{aligned}i_1&=\left(\frac{4\sqrt{26}}{100}\cos(10^5t+\operatorname{arctg}(1/5))-0.1\right)\mathrm A=\tilde i_1-I_0,\\i_2&=\left(\frac{2\sqrt{26}}{100}\cos(10^5t+\operatorname{arctg}(1/5))+0.1\right)\mathrm A=\tilde i_2+I_0.\end{aligned}\tag{2.68}$$

The currents through the coils are the superposition of sinusoidal currents having different amplitudes and a direct current passing only through the coils. This direct current has the constant value

$$I_0=0.1\,\mathrm A\tag{2.69}$$

as in the figure 2.2.

![](p2-sol-fig2)

The alternative currents through the coils has the expressions

$$\tilde i_1=\left(\frac{4\sqrt{26}}{100}\cos(10^5t+\operatorname{arctg}(1/5))\right)\mathrm A,\qquad\tilde i_2=\left(\frac{2\sqrt{26}}{100}\cos(10^5t+\operatorname{arctg}(1/5))\right)\mathrm A.\tag{2.70}$$

The currents through the capacitors has the forms

$$\begin{aligned}i_3&=(-10\times10^{-4}\cdot40\sqrt{26}\cos(10^5t+\operatorname{arctg}(1/5)))\mathrm A,\\i_3&=\left(-\frac{4\sqrt{26}}{100}\cos(10^5t+\operatorname{arctg}(1/5))\right)\mathrm A,\\i_4&=(-5\times10^{-4}\cdot40\sqrt{26}\cos(10^5t+\operatorname{arctg}(1/5)))\mathrm A,\\i_4&=\left(-\frac{2\sqrt{26}}{100}\cos(10^5t+\operatorname{arctg}(1/5))\right)\mathrm A.\end{aligned}\tag{2.71}$$

The current $i_5$ has the expression

$$i_5=i_3-i_1=\left(-\frac{8\sqrt{26}}{100}\cos(10^5t+\operatorname{arctg}(1/5))+0.1\right)\mathrm A.\tag{2.72}$$

The value of the intensity of $i_5$ current is the answer from the question **c**. The initial value of this current is

$$i_5=\left(-\frac{8\sqrt{26}}{100}\frac5{\sqrt{26}}+0.1\right)\mathrm A=-0.3\,\mathrm A.\tag{2.73}$$

problems.title: Optics – Problem III: Prisms
problems.statement:
Two dispersive prisms having apex angles $\hat{A}_1 = 60^{\circ}$ and $\hat{A}_2 = 30^{\circ}$ are glued as in the figure below ( $\hat{C} = 90^{\circ}$ ). The dependences of refraction indexes of the prisms on the wavelength are given by the relations

$$n_1(\lambda) = a_1 + \frac{b_1}{\lambda^2};$$

$$n_2(\lambda) = a_2 + \frac{b_2}{\lambda^2}$$

were

$a_1 = 1{,}1$ , $b_1 = 1 \cdot 10^5\ \mathrm{nm}^2$ , $a_2 = 1{,}3$ , $b_2 = 5 \cdot 10^4\ \mathrm{nm}^2$ .

figures.alt: Two glued prisms forming the rectangle ABCD-like shape: triangle ADC with apex angle A1 at A, refractive index n1, and right triangle ABC with angle A2 at C and index n2, right angle at C; an incident ray arrives from the left on face AD.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Determine the wavelength $\lambda_0$ of the incident radiation that pass through the prisms without refraction on $AC$ face at any incident angle; determine the corresponding refraction indexes of the prisms.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Draw the ray path in the system of prisms for three different radiations $\lambda_{red}$ , $\lambda_0$ , $\lambda_{violet}$ incident on the system at the same angle.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Determine the minimum deviation angle in the system for a ray having the wavelength $\lambda_0$ .

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: Calculate the wavelength of the ray that penetrates and exits the system along directions parallel to DC.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
The ray with the wavelength $\lambda_0$ pass trough the prisms system without refraction on $AC$ face at any angle of incidence if:

$$n_1(\lambda_0)=n_2(\lambda_0).$$

Because the dependence of refraction indexes of prisms on wavelength has the form:

$$n_1(\lambda)=a_1+\frac{b_1}{\lambda^2}\tag{3.1}$$

$$n_2(\lambda)=a_2+\frac{b_2}{\lambda^2}\tag{3.2}$$

The relation (3.1) becomes:

$$a_1+\frac{b_1}{\lambda_0^2}=a_2+\frac{b_2}{\lambda_0^2}.\tag{3.3}$$

The wavelength $\lambda_0$ has correspondingly the form:

$$\lambda_0=\sqrt{\frac{b_1-b_2}{a_2-a_1}}.\tag{3.4}$$

Substituting the furnished numerical values

$$\lambda_0=500\,\mathrm{nm}.\tag{3.5}$$

The corresponding common value of indexes of refraction of prisms for the radiation with the wavelength $\lambda_0$ is:

$$n_1(\lambda_0)=n_2(\lambda_0)=1.5.\tag{3.6}$$

The relations (3.6) and (3.7) represent the answers of question **a**.

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
For the rays with different wavelength $(\lambda_{red},\lambda_0,\lambda_{violet})$ having the same incidence angle on first prism, the paths are illustrated in the figure 1.1.

![](p3-sol-fig1)

The draw illustrated in the figure 1.1 represents the answer of question **b**.

sections.title: c.
sections.statement:
In the figure 1.2 is presented the path of ray with wavelength $\lambda_0$ at minimum deviation (the angle between the direction of incidence of ray and the direction of emerging ray is minimal).

![](p3-sol-fig2)

In this situation

$$n_1(\lambda_0)=n_2(\lambda_0)=\frac{\sin\frac{\delta_{\min}+A'}2}{\sin\frac{A'}2}.\tag{3.7}$$

where $m(\hat A')=30^\circ$, as in the figure 1.1. Substituting in (3.8) the values of refraction indexes the result is

$$\sin\frac{\delta_{\min}+A'}2=\frac32\sin\frac{A'}2\tag{3.8}$$

or

$$\delta_{\min}=2\arcsin\left(\frac32\sin\frac{A'}2\right)-\frac{A'}2.\tag{3.9}$$

Numerically

$$\delta_{\min}\simeq30.7^\circ.\tag{3.10}$$

The relation (3.11) represents the answer of question **c**.

sections.title: d.
sections.statement:
Using the figure 1.3 the refraction law on the $AD$ face is

$$\sin i_1=n_1\sin r_1.\tag{3.11}$$

The refraction law on the $AC$ face is

$$n_1\sin r_1'=n_2\sin r_2.\tag{3.12}$$

![](p3-sol-fig3)

As it can be seen in the figure 1.3

$$r_2=A_2\tag{3.13}$$

and

$$i_1=30^\circ.\tag{3.14}$$

Also,

$$r_1+r_1'=A_1.\tag{3.15}$$

Substituting (3.16) and (3.14) in (3.13) it results

$$n_1\sin(A_1-r_1)=n_2\sin A_2\tag{3.16}$$

or

$$n_1(\sin A_1\cos r_1-\sin r_1\cos A_1)=n_2\sin A_2.\tag{3.17}$$

Because of (3.12) and (3.15) it results that

$$\sin r_1=\frac1{2n_1}\tag{3.18}$$

and

$$\cos r_1=\frac1{2n_1}\sqrt{4n_1^2-1}.\tag{3.19}$$

Putting together the last three relations it results

$$\sqrt{4n_1^2-1}=\frac{2n_2\sin A_2+\cos A_1}{\sin A_1}.\tag{3.20}$$

Because $\hat A_1=60^\circ$ and $\hat A_2=30^\circ$ relation (3.21) can be written as

$$\sqrt{4n_1^2-1}=\frac{2n_2+1}{\sqrt3}\tag{3.21}$$

or

$$3n_1^2=1+n_2+n_2^2.\tag{3.22}$$

Considering the relations (3.1), (3.2) and (3.23) and operating all calculus it results:

$$\lambda^4(3a_1^2-a_2^2-a_2-1)+(6a_1b_1-b_2-2a_2b_2)\lambda^2+3b_1^2-b_2^2=0.\tag{3.23}$$

Solving the equation (3.24) one determine the wavelength $\lambda$ of the ray that enter the prisms system having the direction parallel with $DC$ and emerges the prisms system having the direction again parallel with $DC$. That is

$$\lambda=1194\,\mathrm{nm}\tag{3.24}$$

or

$$\lambda\simeq1.2\,\mu\mathrm m.\tag{3.25}$$

The relation (3.26) represents the answer of question **d**.

*Professor Delia DAVIDESCU, National Department of Evaluation and Examination–Ministry of Education and Research- Bucharest, Romania*

*Professor Adrian S. DAFINEI, PhD, Faculty of Physics – University of Bucharest, Romania*

problems.title: Atomics - Problem IV: Compton scattering
problems.statement:
A photon of wavelength $\lambda_i$ is scattered by a moving, free electron. As a result the electron stops and the resulting photon of wavelength $\lambda_0$ scattered at an angle $\theta = 60^{\circ}$ with respect to the direction of the incident photon, is again scattered by a second free electron at rest. In this second scattering process a photon with wavelength of $\lambda_f = 1{,}25 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$ emerges at an angle $\theta = 60^{\circ}$ with respect to the direction of the photon of wavelength $\lambda_0$ . Find the de Broglie wavelength for the first electron before the interaction. The following constants are known:

$h = 6{,}6 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J \cdot s}$ - Planck’s constant

$m = 9{,}1 \times 10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$ - mass oh the electron

$c = 3{,}0 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$ - speed of light in vacuum

The purpose of the problem is to calculate the values of the speed, momentum and wavelength of the first electron.

To characterize the photons the following notation are used:

*Table 4.1*

|  | initial photon | photon – after the first scattering | final photon |
|---|---|---|---|
| momentum | $\vec{p}_i$ | $\vec{p}_0$ | $\vec{p}_f$ |
| energy | $E_i$ | $E_0$ | $E_f$ |
| wavelength | $\lambda_i$ | $\lambda_i$ | $\lambda_f$ |

To characterize the electrons one uses

*Table 4.2*

|  | first electron before collision | first electron after collision | second electron before collision | Second electron after collision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| momentum | $\vec{p}_{1e}$ | 0 | 0 | $\vec{p}_{2e}$ |
| energy | $E_{1e}$ | $E_{0e}$ | $E_{0e}$ | $E_{2e}$ |
| speed | $\vec{v}_{1e}$ | 0 | 0 | $\vec{v}_{2e}$ |

sections.title: Problem III - Solution
sections.statement:
The purpose of the problem is to calculate the values of the speed, momentum and wavelength of the first electron.

To characterize the photons the following notation are used:

*Table 4.1*

| | initial photon | photon – after the first scattering | final photon |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| momentum | $\vec p_i$ | $\vec p_0$ | $\vec p_f$ |
| energy | $E_i$ | $E_0$ | $E_f$ |
| wavelength | $\lambda_i$ | $\lambda_i$ | $\lambda_f$ |

To characterize the electrons one uses

*Table 4.2*

| | first electron before collision | first electron after collision | second electron before collision | Second electron after collision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| momentum | $\vec p_{1e}$ | $0$ | $0$ | $\vec p_{2e}$ |
| energy | $E_{1e}$ | $E_{0e}$ | $E_{0e}$ | $E_{2e}$ |
| speed | $\vec v_{1e}$ | $0$ | $0$ | $\vec v_{2e}$ |

The image in figure 4.1 presents the situation before the first scattering of photon.

![](p4-sol-fig1)

![](p4-sol-fig2)

![](p4-sol-fig3)

![](p4-sol-fig4)

To characterize the initial photon we will use his momentum $\vec p_i$ and his energy $E_i$

$$\begin{cases}\vec P_i=\dfrac h{\lambda_i}=\dfrac{hf_i}c\\E_i=hf_i\end{cases}\tag{4.1}$$

$$f_i=\frac c{\lambda_i}\tag{4.2}$$

is the frequency of initial photon.

For initial, free electron in motion the momentum $\vec p_{0e}$ and the energy $E_{0e}$ are

$$\begin{cases}\vec P_{0e}=m\vec v_{1e}=\dfrac{m_0\vec v_{1e}}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}\\E_{0e}=mc^2=\dfrac{m_0c^2}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}\end{cases}\tag{4.3}$$

where $m_0$ is the rest mass of electron and $m$ is the mass of moving electron. As usual, $\beta=v_{1e}/c$.

De Broglie wavelength of the first electron is

$$\lambda_{0e}=\frac h{p_{0e}}=\frac h{m_0v_{1e}}\sqrt{1-\beta^2}.$$

The situation after the scattering of photon is described in the figure 4.2. To characterize the scattered photon we will use his momentum $\vec p_0$ and his energy $E_0$

$$\begin{cases}\vec P_0=\dfrac h{\lambda_0}=\dfrac{hf_0}c\\E_0=hf_0\end{cases}\tag{4.4}$$

where

$$f_0=\frac c{\lambda_0}\tag{4.5}$$

is the frequency of scattered photon.

The magnitude of momentum of the electron (that remains in rest) after the scattering is zero; his energy is $E_{1e}$. The mass of electron after collision is $m_0$ - the rest mass of electron at rest. So,

$$E_{1e}=m_0c^2.$$

To determine the moment of the first moving electron, one can write the principles of conservation of moments and energy. That is

$$\vec P_i+\vec p_{0e}=\vec p_0\tag{4.6}$$

and

$$E_i+E_{0e}=E_0+E_{1e}.\tag{4.7}$$

The conservation of moment on $Ox$ direction is written as

$$\frac{hf_i}c+mv_{1e}\cos\alpha=\frac{hf_0}c\cos\theta\tag{4.8}$$

and the conservation of moment on $Oy$ is

$$mv_{1e}\sin\alpha=\frac{hf_0}c\sin\theta.\tag{4.9}$$

To eliminate $\alpha$, the last two equation must be written again as

$$\begin{cases}(mv_{1e}\cos\alpha)^2=\dfrac{h^2}{c^2}(f_0\cos\theta-f_i)^2\\(mv_{1e}\sin\alpha)^2=\left(\dfrac{hf_0}c\sin\theta\right)^2\end{cases}\tag{4.10}$$

and then added. The result is

$$m^2v_{1e}^2=\frac{h^2}{c^2}(f_0^2+f_1^2-2f_0f_i\cos\theta)\tag{4.11}$$

or

$$\frac{m_0^2c^2}{1-(v_{1e}/c)^2}v_{1e}^2=h^2(f_0^2+f_1^2-2f_0f_i\cos\theta).\tag{4.12}$$

The conservation of energy (4.7) can be written again as

$$mc^2+hf_1=m_0c^2+hf_0\tag{4.13}$$

or

$$\frac{m_0c^2}{\sqrt{1-(v_{1e}/c)^2}}=m_0c^2+h(f_0-f_1).\tag{4.14}$$

Squaring the last relation results

$$\frac{m_0^2c^4}{1-(v_{1e}/c)^2}=m_0^2c^4+h^2(f_0-f_1)^2+m_0hc^2(f_0-f_1).\tag{4.15}$$

Subtracting (4.12) from (4.15) the result is

$$2m_0c^2h(f_0-f_1)+2h^2f_1f_0\cos\theta-2h^2f_1f=0\tag{4.16}$$

or

$$\frac h{m_0c}(1-\cos\theta)=\frac c{f_1}-\frac c{f_0}.\tag{4.17}$$

Using

$$\Lambda=\frac h{m_0c}\tag{4.18}$$

the relation (4.17) becomes

$$\Lambda(1-\cos\theta)=\lambda_i-\lambda_0.\tag{4.19}$$

The wavelength of scattered photon is

$$\lambda_0=\lambda_i-\Lambda(1-\cos\theta)\tag{4.20}$$

shorter than the wavelength of initial photon and consequently the energy of scattered photon is greater that the energy of initial photon.

$$\begin{cases}\lambda_i<\lambda_0\\E_i>E_0\end{cases}\tag{4.21}$$

Let's analyze now the second collision process that occurs in point $N$. To study that, let's consider a new referential having $Ox$ direction on the direction of the photon scattered after the first collision.

The figure 4.3 presents the situation before the second collision and the figure 4.4 presents the situation after this scattering process. The conservation principle for moment in the scattering process gives

$$\begin{cases}\dfrac h{\lambda_0}=\dfrac h{\lambda_f}\cos\theta+mv_{2e}\cos\beta\\\dfrac h{\lambda_f}\sin\theta-mv_{2e}\sin\beta=0\end{cases}\tag{4.22}$$

*To eliminate the unknown angle $\beta$ must square and then add the equations (4.22)*

That is

$$\begin{cases}\left(\dfrac h{\lambda_0}-\dfrac h{\lambda_f}\cos\theta\right)^2=(mv_{2e}\cos\beta)^2\\\left(\dfrac h{\lambda_f}\sin\theta\right)^2=(mv_{2e}\sin\beta)^2\end{cases}\tag{4.23}$$

or

$$\left(\frac h{\lambda_f}\right)^2+\left(\frac h{\lambda_0}\right)^2-\frac{2h^2}{\lambda_0\lambda_f}\cos\theta=(mv_{2e})^2.\tag{4.24}$$

The conservation principle of energy in the second scattering process gives

$$\frac{hc}{\lambda_0}+m_0c^2=\frac{hc}{\lambda_f}+mc^2.\tag{4.25}$$

(4.24) and (4.25) gives

$$\frac{h^2c^2}{\lambda_f^2}+\frac{h^2c^2}{\lambda_0^2}-\frac{2h^2c^2}{\lambda_0\lambda_f}\cos\theta=m^2c^2v_{2e}^2\tag{4.26}$$

and

$$h^2c^2\left(\frac1{\lambda_f}-\frac1{\lambda_0}\right)^2+m_0^2c^4+2hc^3m_0\left(\frac1{\lambda_f}-\frac1{\lambda_0}\right)=m^2c^4.\tag{4.27}$$

Subtracting (4.26) from (1.27), one obtain

$$\begin{cases}\dfrac h{m_0c}(1-\cos\theta)=\lambda_f-\lambda_0\\\lambda_f-\lambda_0=\Lambda(1-\cos\theta)\end{cases}\tag{4.28}$$

That is

$$\begin{cases}\lambda_f>\lambda_0\\E_f<E_0\end{cases}\tag{4.29}$$

Because the value of $\lambda_f$ is known and $\Lambda$ can be calculate as

$$\begin{aligned}\lambda_f&=1.25\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm m\\\Lambda&=\frac{6.6\times10^{-34}}{9.1\times10^{-31}\cdot3\times10^8}\,\mathrm m=2.41\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm m=0.02\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm m\end{aligned}\tag{4.30}$$

the value of wavelength of photon before the second scattering is

$$\lambda_0=1.23\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm m.\tag{4.31}$$

Comparing (4.28) written as:

$$\lambda_f=\lambda_0+\Lambda(1-\cos\theta)\tag{4.32}$$

and (4.20) written as

$$\lambda_i=\lambda_0+\Lambda(1-\cos\theta)\tag{4.33}$$

clearly results

$$\lambda_i=\lambda_f.\tag{4.34}$$

The energy of the double scattered photon is the same as the energy of initial photon. The direction of “final photon” is the same as the direction of “initial” photon. Concluding, the final photon is identical with the initial photon. The result is expected because of the symmetry of the processes.

Extending the symmetry analyze on electrons, the first moving electron that collides the initial photon and after that remains at rest must have the same moment and energy as the second electron after the collision – because this second electron is at rest before the collision.

That is

$$\begin{cases}\vec p_{1e}=\vec p_{2e}\\E_{1e}=E_{2e}\end{cases}\tag{4.35}$$

Taking into account (4.24), the moment of final electron is

$$p_{2e}=h\sqrt{\frac1{\lambda_f^2}+\frac1{(\lambda_f-\Lambda(1-\cos\theta))^2}-\frac{2\cos\theta}{\lambda_f(\lambda_f-\Lambda(1-\cos\theta))}}.\tag{4.36}$$

The de Broglie wavelength of second electron after scattering (and of first electron before scattering) is

$$\lambda_{1e}=\lambda_{2e}=\frac1{\sqrt{\frac1{\lambda_f^2}+\frac1{(\lambda_f-\Lambda(1-\cos\theta))^2}-\frac{2\cos\theta}{\lambda_f(\lambda_f-\Lambda(1-\cos\theta))}}}.\tag{4.37}$$

Numerical value of this wavelength is

$$\lambda_{1e}=\lambda_{2e}=1.24\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm m.\tag{4.38}$$

*Professor Delia DAVIDESCU, National Department of Evaluation and Examination–Ministry of Education and Research- Bucharest, Romania*

*Professor Adrian S. DAFINEI, PhD, Faculty of Physics – University of Bucharest, Romania*

problems.title: IPhO’s LOGO – Problem V
problems.statement:
The Logo of the International Physics Olympiad is represented in the figure below.

The figure presents the phenomenon of the curving of the trajectory of a jet of fluid around the shape of a cylindrical surface. The trajectory of fluid is not like the expected dashed line but as the circular solid line.

Qualitatively explain this phenomenon (first observed by Romanian engineer Henry Coanda in 1936).

*This problem will be not considered in the general score of the Olympiad. The best solution will be awarded a special prize.*

sections.title: Problem V - Solution
sections.statement:
Suppose a fluid is in a recipient at a constant pressure. If a thin jet of fluid (gas or liquid) having a small circular or rectangular cross section leaves the recipient through a nozzle entering the medium, the particles belonging to the medium will be carried out by the jet. Other particles belonging to the medium will be attracted to the jet.

If the jet flows over a large surface, the particles belonging to the medium over the jet and the particles leaving between the jet and the surface will be carried out by the jet. The density of particles over the jet remains constant because of newly arriving particles, but the particles between the surface and the jet cannot be replaced. A pressure difference appears between the upper and lower side of the jet, pushing the jet to the surface. If the surface is curved, the jet will follow its shape.

The left image in the figure below presents the normal flow of a fluid jet leaving through a nozzle of a recipient with a high, constant pressure. The final pressure of the fluid is of medium pressure.

The right image in the figure below presents the flow of a fluid over the large surface. The jet is “stuck” against the surface.

![](p5-sol-fig1)

The process of deflection of the jet increases the speed of the jet without any variation of the pressure and temperature of the jet.

During the tests of the first jet plane in Paris, December 1936, the Romanian engineer Henry Coanda was the first to observe this phenomenon, occurring when the flames of the engine passed through a flap.

The logo of the Olympiad illustrates the Coanda flow of a fluid.
